share_verdict: Your idli is a rice cake. It did not begin as one.
translation: The split black gram, soaked … the husks [removed] by rubbing with the hands. Then, having ground [them] on the grinding-stone, mixed with seasonings, kneaded many times in a pot, he should set it aside from the hand. The soured black-gram paste he should put into vaṭikās. Covering with others [containing] valla-cores, he should cook it thoroughly. Taking it down, he should scatter powdered pepper on top. Smeared with ghee, he should fumigate it with asafoetida-and-ghee and with cumin. Well-cooled, white, smooth — these are the excellent iḍḍarikās.

ingredients.name: urad dal, split and dehusked
ingredients.function: the entire batter. Zero rice, the ancient idli is 100% urad, which is why it was dense, soft and custardy rather than light and open

ingredients.name: asafoetida water
ingredients.function: seasoning and digestive, worked into the batter rather than sprinkled on

ingredients.name: black pepper, powdered
ingredients.function: scattered over after cooking, not mixed in

ingredients.name: ghee
ingredients.function: smeared on the cooked cakes, then used with asafoetida and cumin to fumigate them

method_reconstructed: Soak split black gram and rub off the husks by hand.
Grind on the grinding-stone, mix in the seasonings, and knead many times in a pot.
Set it aside until the paste has soured, the text is explicit that it is soured before moulding.
Spoon into vaṭikā moulds, cover with other vessels, and cook through.
Take off the heat, scatter powdered pepper over, smear with ghee.
Fumigate with asafoetida-ghee and cumin. Serve well-cooled, white and smooth.
contested_points: The passage describes a soured urad paste, so the batter was fermented, but it says nothing about rice, and the modern 2:1 to 3:1 rice-to-urad batter has no basis in it.
The cakes were served cooled, not hot from the steamer.

changed.to: 65–75% polished rice, with urad reduced to a fermenting agent
changed.driver: polished rice became the cheapest and most available grain in South Indian kitchens; mechanised milling made it keep, and post-Independence procurement and public distribution centred on rice and wheat

changed.from: pepper, asafoetida, ginger and cumin worked through the dish
changed.to: a plain, unseasoned batter with the flavour moved to the accompaniments
changed.driver: the dish became a vehicle for sambar and chutney rather than a seasoned item in its own right

ingredients: 2 cups whole urad dal (gota urad), soaked 6 hours
1/4 tsp asafoetida dissolved in 2 tbsp water
2 tbsp ghee, and a pinch of cumin
steps: Grind the soaked dal with as little cold water as you can manage, until white and fluffy.
Work in the asafoetida water, ginger and salt. Cover and leave 8–12 hours somewhere warm, until it smells sour.
Fill greased moulds three-quarters full, cover, and steam 12–14 minutes.
Scatter powdered pepper over, smear with ghee, and finish with cumin.
Let them cool before eating, the text is specific about that, and a cooled 100% urad cake is a different thing from a hot rice idli.
Denser and custardy, and it tastes of dal and pepper rather than of nothing.

verification.note: Passage located and translated in the editorial extraction, dated 1129 CE. The Devanagari has not yet been transcribed into this record, so the source drawer shows the translation and says so.
